title: Synonyms & Antonyms
intro: Synonyms (same meaning) and antonyms (opposite meaning) are the most direct vocabulary marks in SSC — you either know the word or you don't, so the work is building a strong word bank. The smart way is not rote lists but learning words in families and from roots: knowing that 'bene-' means good unlocks benevolent, beneficial and benefactor at once. This chapter shows the method and drills the high-frequency words SSC repeats.

formulas.title: How to attack a vocab question

items.name: Use context
items.formula: recall the word in a sentence you have seen

items.name: Eliminate
items.formula: remove options that are clearly unrelated first

items.name: Watch the question
items.formula: synonym vs antonym — read which is asked

topics.name: Synonyms
topics.details: A synonym is a word with the same or nearly the same meaning. When you don't know a word, break it into a root/prefix or recall it in a familiar phrase, then match the closest option. Beware near-synonyms that differ in strength.

topics.name: Antonyms
topics.details: An antonym is a word opposite in meaning. Many antonyms are formed by prefixes — un-, in-, dis-, non-, mis-. For root words, recall the meaning and pick the option that reverses it. Watch out for options that are merely different (not opposite).

topics.name: Shades of Meaning
topics.details: Words that look like synonyms can differ in degree, formality or connotation. 'Thin', 'slim' and 'skinny' all describe low body weight, but slim is positive, skinny negative. SSC tests whether you pick the option that matches both the meaning AND the tone.

solved.problem: Which is a positive word for "thin": slim or skinny?
Childish vs childlike — which is complimentary?
Famous vs notorious — which is negative?
Which is stronger: angry or furious?

unsolved.problem: Confident vs arrogant — which is negative?
Which is stronger: like or adore?
Economical vs stingy — which is positive?
Curious vs nosy — which is negative?
Which is a negative word for "thin"?

topics.name: Commonly Confused Words
topics.details: Pairs that sound or look alike trip candidates: 'affect' (verb) vs 'effect' (noun); 'principal' (head/main) vs 'principle' (a rule); 'stationary' (not moving) vs 'stationery' (writing materials). Learn each pair with a one-line memory cue.

solved.problem: Affect or effect: "The rain will ___ the match."
Principal or principle: "Honesty is a good ___."
Stationary or stationery: "He bought pens from the ___ shop."
Complement or compliment: "She paid him a nice ___."

shortcuts: Learn words by roots/prefixes (bene-, mal-, anti-, un-, dis-) — one root unlocks many words.
Match meaning AND intensity/tone, not just rough sense.
For antonyms, look for prefix forms (visible → invisible) first.
Read whether a synonym or an antonym is asked — the trap is answering the wrong one.
Eliminate clearly unrelated options before deciding.
mistakes: Answering a synonym when an antonym is asked (and vice versa).
Picking a near-synonym of the wrong intensity (angry vs furious).
Choosing a merely "different" word instead of the true opposite.
pyq: SSC Tier 1 asks 2–3 synonyms and 2–3 antonyms of moderate words, plus one or two confused-word items in fill-in-the-blank form. A steadily built word bank turns these into quick marks.
summary: Synonyms and antonyms reward a word bank built from roots and context, not rote lists. Match both meaning and tone, use prefixes to form opposites, and keep look-alike pairs (affect/effect, principal/principle) straight. Always check whether the question wants the same or the opposite meaning.
